question.text: A projectile is launched with speed 2√(gh). It just skims over two walls, each of height h, separated from each other by a distance 2h. Prove that the duration it spends traveling between the two walls equals 2√(h/g). As a method hint: first work out the speed at height h, then treat that as a fresh initial speed with 2h as the range.
conditions: particle projected so it just grazes the tops of both walls
the two walls are of equal height h
the walls are separated by a distance 2h

solution.approach: The horizontal velocity stays constant, and the speed at the wall-crossing height satisfies a mini-projectile range condition that forces the horizontal and vertical velocities there to be equal.

steps.text: The horizontal velocity component never changes during flight, so the speed at height h relates to the launch speed through the usual height-velocity equation.
Treat the point where the particle first reaches height h as a new launch point. It returns to the same height h after a horizontal distance of 2h, exactly like a projectile range.
Combine the two relations above; they force the horizontal and vertical velocities at height h to be equal.
steps.equation: vₓ² + v_y1² = 2gh and vₓv_y1 = gh ⟹ (vₓ − v_y1)² = 0 ⟹ vₓ = v_y1 = √(gh)

steps.text: The time between the walls is the flight time of the mini-projectile, which is twice the vertical velocity at height h divided by g.

common_mistakes.text: Using the full launch speed u in place of the horizontal velocity between the walls gives t = 2h/u, which is exactly half the correct time.
